artwork_title: Présentation de la Vierge au Temple
provenance: A private Belgian collection, by whom sold | Sale Lepke, Berlin 25 April 1911, lot 131 (as 'Isembrant') | Possibly Baron Kerssenbrock (according to an hand written note by Friedländer on the reverse of RKD photo 32516 (Annunciation - 'm. einem / zweiten / Flügel') | French Art Market, where purchased by the present owner around 2000 | | Jean Bellegambe, active in his native Douai and across the County of Flanders, stands among the most sophisticated painters of the early sixteenth century in the Franco‑Flemish world. His art reflects the rich interplay of influences from Bruges, Antwerp, and Valenciennes, blending conservative devotional tradition with the refined elegance and jewel‑like palette characteristic of the region's finest workshops. | The present panel originally formed the fourth element of a five‑part polyptych narrating the Life of the Virgin, a work formerly given to 'Isembrandt' (see sale, 1911) but attributed by Max J. Friedländer to Jean Bellegambe, as noted in his own hand on the reverse of a photograph of the complete ensemble preserved in the RKD Institute (inv. 32516). The reconstructed sequence is: | Annunciation (far left); Visitation; Adoration of the Christ Child by the Virgin, Saint Joseph and five angels, with the Annunciation to the Shepherds in the background (centre, immediately to the left of our panel); Presentation of Christ in the Temple (the present panel) and the Assumption of the Virgin with the Apostles gathered around her sarcophagus below as angels bear her heavenward (far right). | | The upper contours of the compositions originally followed the silhouette of a carved Gothic framework, now removed from our panel, though its outline remains clearly visible under raking light—evidence of its original integration within a unified architectural setting. | Although the complete polyptych was still recorded in 1911, no further trace of the missing panels has come to light since then, and their current whereabouts remain unknown. The present painting reappeared independently on the French art market, where it was acquired by the current owner as a work by Jean Maisoncelles (circa 1436-1479) (the attribution presumably made in connection with works at the Chartreuse de Champmol). | Despite a few localized restorations, the painting retains striking freshness of colour, with passages that preserve much of their original brilliance. Notably, in several areas the paint surface reveals the underdrawing, showing the artist's precise preparatory method. | Bellegambe's oeuvre is traditionally divided into two phases. His early style (c. 1508–1525) is rooted in the archaizing tradition of Valenciennes, shaped by artists such as Simon Marmion and Jan Provost, whose workshop he may have known. His later works—to which the present panel most closely relates—show a measured assimilation of Antwerp mannerism, with broadened spatial organisation, heightened chromatic contrasts, and greater narrative vitality, yet retain the compositional clarity favoured by his monastic patrons. Friedländer long ago noted Bellegambe's stylistic proximity to painters active in Antwerp and Bruges, an influence fully evident here in the graceful figures, brillant palette, and delicate modelling. | With its refined execution, luminous colour, visible underdrawing, and survival outside the now‑lost ensemble, this panel constitutes an interesting fragment of a significant lost polyptych and offers valuable insight into the development of devotional painting in the Franco‑Flemish world in the early sixteenth century.

provenance: Sale, Kohn, Paris, 6 December 1999, lot 1, (sold for € 111,288 (FRF 730,000)), where purchased by the present owner | Private collection, France |  |  | Sebastiaen Vrancx, the pioneering Flemish master of cavalry and battle painting, developed a distinctive visual language combining acute observational realism with a carefully constructed, architectural sense of space. Born in Antwerp and trained under Adam van Noort (1562–1641), who also taught Rubens and Jordaens, Vrancx absorbed the rigorous draughtsmanship of the Antwerp Mannerist tradition before refining his approach during several formative years in Italy, where he encountered the perspectival and landscape innovations of Paul Bril (ca. 1554–1626). | Dated 1625, the present painting comes from his fully mature phase, when the artist's battle scenes became increasingly sophisticated in the choreography of horses, tonal subtlety, and clarity of narrative. The artist's ability to organise densely populated cavalry encounters along strong diagonal axes—here cutting through a Flemish village street—reveals the same compositional devices seen in comparable works of the 1620s. A defining feature of Vrancx's oeuvre is his ability to render the movement of horses, a skill that secured his role as one of the founders of the Flemish cavalry‑battle genre, later influencing painters such as Pieter Snayers (1592-1667) and Adam Frans van der Meulen (1632-1690). |  | At the time of the Kohn sale, it was noted that the present lot was due to be included in Joost Vander Auwera's forthcoming catalogue of the artist's works, which is still in preparation.

P. 471); the other showing, on the same canvas, two orientations of the bust—one in profile facing right, the other in a slight three-quarter turn to the left (Paris, Musée du Louvre, originally an oval oil on canvas. These three poses were intended for his friend, the sculptor Antoine Coysevox, from whom the painter had commissioned a marble portrait of his mother; it was not completed until 1706 (Paris, Musée du Louvre, marble, H. 0.83 m; H. with pedestal 1.59 m; depth 0.28 m, inv. L.P. 502). Four years earlier, in 1702, Rigaud had entrusted another close associate, the engraver Pierre Drevet, with reproducing the frontal portrait of Maria Serra, adorning the print with a dedicatory inscription imbued with filial devotion ("aeternum pietatis monumentum"). | Executed as a counterpart to the Fontaine-Henry canvas and following the same orientation as Drevet's engraving, the drawing presented here focuses on the sitter's features and the principal elements of her clothing, which correspond to the traditional dress of Roussillon's artisan women: a bodice rounded both front and back, fitted with straps beneath which the white fichu passes, forming small wing-like extensions on each side. The velvet veil—something of a Riguadian signature in textile matters—recalls the head coverings of Rembrandt's elderly women (for example, Oxford, Ashmolean Museum, The Royal Collection, inv. RCIN 405000), an artist Rigaud admired fervently. The use of black chalk with white heightening aligns with the technique Rigaud favored in most of his sheets, many of which are preparatory—sometimes squared, sometimes not—for the translation of his most notable portraits by his appointed engravers such as Pierre Drevet. | The economy of means with which the physiognomy is rendered in all its subtlety—note, in this respect, the full brow, the sharpness of the gaze, the small highlight at the tip of the nose, the modelling of the cheeks, lips, chin, and neck—together with the illusionistic softness of the velvet atop the head, is characteristic of the artist. Equally typical is the particularly firm, somewhat drier and quicker manner in which Rigaud customarily guided the engraver's forthcoming work, indicating explicitly where the tool should press more incisively and where the shadows should be emphasized and deepened. These elements support, in our view, the hypothesis that this is a preparatory drawing for the engraving, rather than a copy after the print—especially since our drawing differs from the engraving in several respects, including its tighter framing and plain background, not to mention the absence of the feigned frame present in the print, which must certainly have been the subject of another drawing by Rigaud. | | We are grateful to Ariane James-Sarazin for her assistance in compiling this catalogue note.

provenance: Private collection, US | | | As a master of still life and an academician of the Imperial Academy of Arts in Saint Petersburg, Khrutsky consistently adhered to the artistic traditions of the old European masters. His works closely resemble the still-life paintings of the Dutch artists of the 17th century. | | In Khrutsky's still lifes, the genre traditions adopted from European models are preserved, but they are reinterpreted in accordance with the painter's contemporary ideas about the meaning of an artistic image. Motifs placed in a modern context are almost completely deprived of symbolic meaning. | | Exotic fruits - lemons, grapes, peaches appear alongside fruits familiar to residents of central Russia such as apples, currants, cherries, and strawberries. In his bouquets, roses and carnations do not dominate; instead, garden peonies prevail. | | In the foreground of Khrutsky's paintings one can often see a characteristic element of the traditional Dutch 'luxurious breakfast' still life: a lemon with its peel cut into a spiral. Next to it appear rough, simple vegetables. | | The combination of everyday reality with the classical harmony of pictorial imagery is particularly expressive in still lives where, instead of delicate flowers and juicy fruits, simple kitchen utensils, vegetables, and mushrooms 'pose' as the main subjects. | | The presented painting Still Life with Mushrooms was created in the early 1850s. Several similar works exist, since the artist preferred the genre of still life to the more common and 'prestigious' directions of the time - landscape and historical painting. In Still Life with Mushrooms, Ivan Khrutsky adopted the technical foundation of 17th-century Dutch painting while infusing it with a distinctly different emotional tone. While Western European still lives were often imbued with a sense of satiation and the lifelessness associated with it, Khrutsky's work appears abundant, lively, and optimistic. The stability of the baskets is juxtaposed with the apparent messiness of the various forest mushrooms, creating a composition that is both dynamic and balanced. The warm colour scheme and dark background also refer to the traditions of Western European still-life painting.

provenance: With Schweitzer Gallery, New York (according to the stamps on the reverse) | Sale, Duran , Madrid 18 October 1994, lot 46 | Private collection, Spain | | This elegant Venetian view by Martín Rico y Ortega depicts gondolas gliding across the Giudecca Canal before the luminous façade and domes of the Basilica del Redentore, designed by Andrea Palladio (1508–1580). Groups of figures animate the foreground, embarking and conversing along the water's edge, while the calm surface of the lagoon reflects the soft light of the Venetian sky. | | Born in Madrid, Rico trained at the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando and later worked in Paris, where he came into contact with the landscape painter Charles-François Daubigny (1817–1878) and the Barbizon circle. After discovering Venice in the 1860s, he returned frequently and eventually settled there, producing the luminous canal views that secured his international reputation. His paintings were widely exhibited and collected across Europe and the United States. | | Rico repeatedly painted the most celebrated sites of Venice, including views of the Grand Canal with Santa Maria della Salute, lively scenes of the Piazzetta San Marco, and tranquil canals lined with weathered palazzi and animated by gondolas. The present work is characteristic of his mature Venetian production, combining topographical accuracy with a poetic sensitivity to light and atmosphere.

provenance: Sale, Pillon, Calais, 12 December 2004, lot 57 | Private collection, France | | A prominent figure in late 19th‑century French academic painting, Léon Bazille Perrault was admired for his refined technique and his tender portrayals of childhood and allegorical subjects. Trained under François‑Édouard Picot (1786–1868) and later William‑Adolphe Bouguereau (1825–1905), he absorbed the disciplined classicism and luminous finish that define the academic tradition. His work also carries echoes of earlier French masters such as Jean‑Antoine Watteau (1684–1721) and François Boucher (1703–1770). | | A regular Salon exhibitor from 1861, Perrault quickly gained success with paintings that appealed to the 19th‑century taste for beauty, sentiment and idealisation. He received an honourable mention in 1864, a second‑class medal in 1876, and was appointed Chevalier de la Légion d'Honneur in 1887. | | Painted in 1888, the present work is characteristic of Perrault's celebrated vision of childhood. The figures are visually emphasized by a surrounding golden painted border, an element that introduces a quasi‑devotional framework to the image. Although Perrault commonly presented his works in ornate gilded frames, the available sources do not identify other examples in which he incorporated a painted gilded border directly onto the canvas. In Le sommeil des anges, this device therefore appears to be exceptional and may be understood within academic practices that used visual framing to enhance the compositional and thematic elevation of a work.

artwork_title: Jeune italien à la source, Narcisse
provenance: From the Artist's studio | Marie-Anne Tower-Rosen-Feydeau (eldest daughter of the artist) | M. Bureau, Paris, 1973 | The Collection of Jacques Seligmann, Paris and thence by descent | Private collection, France | | Exhibited | Paris, Ecole des Beaux-Arts, Exposition des oeuvres de Louis François, 1898, no 241 | Paris, Musée national du Luxembourg, Carolus-Duran, 1919, no 14 (as Enfant italien sur fond de paysage and dated 1824) | Paris, Galerie Marcel Flavian, Carolus-Duran 1837-1917, no 28, 12 June-16 July 1973 (dated 1864) | Lille, Palais des Beaux-Arts, Carolus-Duran 1837-1917, no. 9, 27 June-29 September 2003 | | Literature | Inventaire après-décès des tableaux de Carolus-Duran établi par Léonce Bénédite le 7 avril 1921, No 46 (as Enfant italien nu) | Le Gal, Carolus-Duran, sa vie, son oeuvre dessiné, thèse inédite de l'école du Louvre sous la direction de Roseline Bacou, Paris, 1973, vol. I, pp. 28, 34, no 20. | | Painted in 1863, the present work stands as an eloquent testament to the young Carolus‑Duran's early ambitions, created during the formative years that preceded his emergence as one of the foremost portraitists of the Third Republic. | Executed during his sojourn in Italy—and in Rome in particular—the painting reveals the artist's expanding mastery of chiaroscuro and his growing fascination with the psychological presence of his sitters. In this refined interpretation of a classical theme, Carolus‑Duran turns away from grand, narrative mythmaking and instead captures an intimate, contemplative moment. The young Italian boy is rendered with the heightened naturalism and sculptural solidity characteristic of the artist's early oeuvre. The figure, seated on the riverbank, looking down at his image reflected in the water, may also be read as a Narcissus‑like youth, situating the work within the mid‑19th‑century French revival of mythological subjects reimagined through a modern, humanised sensibility. | Rare in subject within Carolus‑Duran's production, the canvas offers a revealing glimpse into the painter's artistic evolution in the early 1860s, bridging the academic rigor of his training and the expressive freedom that would later define his mature style—an approach that would, in turn, influence an entire generation, including his most celebrated pupil, John Singer Sargent. | The notable provenance of the painting further underscores its importance: retained initially in the artist's own collection and then inherited by his eldest daughter, it subsequently passed to Mr. Bureau before entering the hands of the distinguished dealer Jacques Seligmann. Seligmann's galleries in Paris and New York were instrumental in shaping leading European and American collections in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and works handled by him are often marked by their historical significance and exceptional quality. | | The attribution of this painting to Carolus-Duran (1837-1917) has been confirmed by Brame & Lorenceau following a physical examination of the work; it now features in their archives on the artist.
